deep.reconstruction:
Context: E477 studies the 'singular series' q^m = Σ_{k≥1} k^{-m}(1+2^{-n}+…+k^{-n}) = Σ H_k^{(n)}/k^m, i.e. ζ(m,n)+ζ(λ) in modern double-zeta notation, of 'order' (weight) λ=m+n. Euler writes p^s for ζ(s) and a(b) for the binomial coefficient C(a,b). The proof of this reading is his own remark (λ-1)(n-1)+(λ-1)(m-1)=λ(n)=λ(m), which is Pascal's rule C(λ-1,n-1)+C(λ-1,n)=C(λ,n), together with symmetry.

This page finishes §37, Euler's evaluation of all odd-weight linear sums. Case II (m odd) has no ζ(m)ζ(n) term (the '*'). It reads q^m = ½(1−C(λ,n))ζ(λ) plus bracket terms [C(2k,n−1)+C(2k,m−1)] attached to ζ(2k+1), for k=0,…,(λ−3)/2. The companion even factor ζ(λ−1−2k) is implicit in the printed layout.

A uniform statement of the correct result is:
q^m = [(1+(−1)^m)/2]ζ(m)ζ(n) + ½(1+(−1)^m C(λ,m))ζ(λ) − (−1)^m Σ_{k=0}^{(λ−3)/2} [C(2k,m−1)+C(2k,n−1)] ζ(2k+1)ζ(λ−1−2k).
Checks:
- m=2, n=1: 2ζ(3).
- m=4, n=1: 3ζ(5)−ζ(2)ζ(3).
- m=2, n=3: (11/2)ζ(5)−2ζ(2)ζ(3).
- m=3, n=2: 3ζ(2)ζ(3)−(9/2)ζ(5), numerically about 1.266. The direct partial sum 1 + 1.25/8 + … ≈ 1.27 agrees.

Euler's closing remark: continuing the pattern one step gives the term k=(λ−1)/2, with coefficient C(λ−1,n−1)+C(λ−1,m−1)=C(λ,n), multiplying ζ(λ)·p^0. With ζ(0)=−½, that term is ∓½C(λ,n)ζ(λ). This is exactly the binomial part of the ζ(λ) coefficient. So the isolated ½(1±C(λ,n))p^λ term is the natural continuation of the bracket series; the remark explains its origin.

§38: for even λ these formulas fail. Euler gives his reason: in the odd case, symmetry p^m·p^n couples odd- and even-indexed zetas, which does not happen in the even case. His three methods (stuffle-type symmetry, partial fractions, etc.) do not determine the even-order sums. The third method already fails to give all determinations at order 8. Orders 4 and 6 were evaluated earlier, but no general law is visible. His explanation: for even orders any two of ζ(λ), ζ(2), ζ(4), … are commensurable (rational multiples of π-powers). Hence the linear relations his methods generate collapse and too few independent equations remain. On the next page he nevertheless asserts there is 'no doubt' other methods exist to sum the even orders.
errors:
Sign discrepancy. If each bracket term means +[C(2k,n−1)+C(2k,m−1)]·ζ(2k+1)ζ(λ−1−2k), the printed minus signs in Case II give the wrong sign. For m=3, n=2 it yields −(9/2)ζ(5)−3ζ(2)ζ(3)<0, whereas the true value is 3ζ(2)ζ(3)−(9/2)ζ(5).
- Correct convention: the bracket terms carry sign −(−1)^m, i.e. negative for m even (Case I) and positive for m odd (Case II).
- Case I needs negative signs, e.g. so that the ζ(1)ζ(2) divergences cancel for m=2, n=1.
- The previous-page transcription shows '+' in Case I, so the signs of the two cases appear interchanged (misprint, or a convention not visible here). I am unsure whether the Opera omnia editors flag this.
Case II with m=1 is formally divergent (Σ H_k^{(n)}/k); the formula is meaningful only for m≥2, n≥2 (Case I covers n=1 via cancellation).

Euler's conjecture that other methods will sum all even orders is, in modern understanding, false. Double zeta values such as ζ(6,2) of weight 8 are believed (not proved) to be irreducible to products of single zeta values.

ideas.what: Closed evaluation of all odd-weight linear Euler sums Σ H_k^{(n)}/k^m in terms of ζ(λ) and products ζ(odd)ζ(even), with binomial coefficients
ideas.modern_name: Euler's theorem on double zeta values of odd weight (depth-2 reduction)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E477, 1776); rigorous modern proofs by Borwein–Borwein–Girgensohn (1995), Flajolet–Salvy (1998)

ideas.what: Observation that the next term in the pattern has coefficient C(λ,n), linking it to the separate ½C(λ,n)ζ(λ) term; implicitly the term with ζ(0)=−1/2
ideas.modern_name: Uniform formula for odd-weight double zetas including the k=(λ−1)/2 term with ζ(0)=−1/2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in modern uniform statements (e.g. Borwein–Girgensohn, Zagier-style formulas)

ideas.what: Failure of the methods for even weight, first incomplete at weight 8; weights 4 and 6 fully evaluable; reason attributed to commensurability of even zeta values
ideas.modern_name: Irreducibility of even-weight double zeta values (first at weight 8, e.g. ζ(6,2)); dimension of the double-zeta space / Broadhurst–Kreimer
ideas.usually_credited_to: Broadhurst–Kreimer (1997), Gangl–Kaneko–Zagier (2006), Borwein–Girgensohn (1996) for the modern picture

missed.claim: Euler explicitly notes that the 'next' term of the bracket series has coefficient C(λ,n), matching the ζ(λ) coefficient. Read with ζ(0)=−1/2 (a value Euler knew from E352), this hints at a single uniform sum over k including the endpoint, rather than an isolated ½(1±C(λ,n))ζ(λ) term. Euler does not carry it out.
missed.quote: Secundum hanc legem terminus vltimum sequens fieret (λ-1)(n-1), (λ-1)(m-1) } p^λ, vbi notetur semper esse (λ-1)(n-1)+(λ-1)(m-1)=λ(n)=λ(m).
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical anticipation of the regularized/uniform form of the odd-weight double zeta formula; it is minor, as modern statements already absorb this term.

missed.claim: Euler pinpoints weight 8 as the first even order where his methods leave determinations undetermined, while weights 4 and 6 are complete. This matches the modern fact that weight 8 is where an irreducible double zeta value (ζ(6,2)/ζ(5,3)) first appears. Specialists in the MZV literature know E477, but this specific 'order 8' remark is rarely highlighted.
missed.quote: cum etiam tertia pro ordine octauo non omnes determinationes suppeditet
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical precursor to the depth-2 irreducibility phenomenon; it is mainly of historiographic interest.

deep.surprise_reason: The main result (odd-weight Euler sums) is famous and credited to E477. Two details are mildly interesting: the remark that the 'next term' reproduces the C(λ,n)ζ(λ) coefficient (implicitly ζ(0)=−1/2), and the precise identification of order 8 as the first failure, which coincides with the first irreducible double zeta. There is also an apparent sign inconsistency in the printed cases.
transcription_corrections: The machine transcription matches the image; the minus signs in Case II brackets are indeed printed as '−'.
'nou sufficiunt' in the scan is a printing typo for 'non sufficiunt' (transcription already normalizes it).
In the first line, 'p^λ' is followed by the bracket '−0(n−1)/−0(m−1)' that belongs to the next factor p (p^1), not to the exponent of p^λ.
